lessons.title: UI lab: build a synthetic booking draft end to end
lessons.summary: Build one small draft flow with shared state, a picker, a review screen, and clear checks.
objectives: Build a UI from written behavior rules rather than copying a production feature.
Keep one observable draft and share it with editors and the review screen.
Combine a modal picker, pushed review, UIKit message, and work tied to the review view.
Record what you checked and compare your scratch owners with the active demo.

sections.title: Write what the draft flow must do
sections.html:
A draft is an unfinished choice the user can still edit. Build a small made-up visit draft in a separate iOS learning target. It has a display name, a selected reason, Review, and Reset. A modal picker changes the reason only when you choose one; Cancel keeps the old choice. Review reads the same draft and displays a UIKit message. A synthetic async result lets you practise waiting without calling a backend.

This is a UI and ownership lab, not an appointment-booking implementation. Use labels such as Demo chat and Demo check-in, and do not enter patient details. No code in the client checkout needs to change. The worked solution is supplied as reference material to inspect after your attempt; the course author has not created or run your app for you.

Write the acceptance contract first. Review is disabled when the trimmed display name is empty or no reason is selected. A modal cancel never clears a valid prior selection. Returning from Review preserves edits while the root identity remains. Reset clears the model's draft fields explicitly. Unrelated rendering must not start a second picker or recreate the model. These statements give you stronger checkpoints than merely asking whether the UI looks familiar.

sections.title: Set up one scratch app and its test targets
sections.html:
Deployment support is the oldest OS your app promises to run on. Choose iOS 17 or later for this Observation lab, then check your toolchain and language mode separately. If you inspect or run existing demo fixtures, read their scheme and dependencies first. This checkout has both Tuist manifests and a checked-in Xcode project. The manifest uses a migration suffix. Do not assume the two build routes have identical settings.

Your scratch files need target membership in the app; behavior tests need membership in a unit-test target, and UI automation belongs in a UI-test target. A Swift source file visible in the project navigator is not proof that it belongs to the right module. Imports describe module dependencies, not directories. Keep the lab's types internal to the scratch module unless a separate target has a deliberate reason to expose them.

Set one SwiftUI root from your app entry point. The @main attribute identifies the executable entry type, and an App body supplies scenes such as a WindowGroup. Do not add a second @main type to the same app target. A preview is a development rendering context, not proof that scene setup, navigation, lifecycle, and test-host behavior all work when the app launches.

sections.title: Give the draft one owner
sections.html:
A source of truth is the place holding the current value everyone else reads. Use one Observable, MainActor class for the draft and keep it in the root's State. The editor, picker, and review receive that same object. Use Bindable when controls need bindings. Picker buttons can assign through a plain reference. Do not copy the name and reason into separate stores on each screen.

The made-up reasons form a finite String raw-value enum. CaseIterable supplies allCases, the list of cases. Identifiable supplies each row's stable identity. In var id: Self { self }, Self means this type, and the returned enum value identifies the row. A later display-label edit therefore need not make the row a different choice.

The optional selectedReason models absence honestly. Optional chaining such as selectedReason?.rawValue reads a label only when a selection exists; ?? supplies a fallback. A computed canReview derives eligibility from the current fields. Do not maintain a separate validity flag with callbacks from multiple controls. Your Android counterpart would be one immutable UI-state stream or one shared state holder with derived validity; the exact Observation mechanics remain different.

sections.title: Build one working checkpoint at a time
sections.html:
A checkpoint is one small behavior you can verify before adding the next. First, bind a text field to the draft and show derived eligibility. Spaces alone must leave eligibility false. Next, add a modal picker. The root owns whether it is shown; the picker reads dismiss within its own presentation. Its NavigationStack supplies its title and Cancel toolbar in this separate modal scope.

Third, add Review to the root stack. A destination-based NavigationLink is enough for this small lab. Use lesson 010's typed path when you need programmatic routing or restoration. Disable the link for an incomplete draft. A disabled control helps the user, but does not replace validation at a real submission boundary. That boundary must check its own inputs.

Checkpoint four inserts UIKitMessage from session 010. Give it a changing String from the draft and confirm that its update method applies current input to the existing controller. Set a suitable frame for this small message in a Form row so its intended height is explicit. Avoid making the controller report selection or validation merely because its displayed message updated.

Checkpoint five adds DemoLoadingScreen from session 011 using a synthetic reason label as its ID. It directly awaits its model load in a task modifier. This demonstrates that a screen-associated task belongs to the Review presentation, while the draft belongs to the root.

sections.title: Check values and real interactions separately
sections.html:
A model test checks draft rules directly, without tapping a simulator screen. Cover empty, spaces-only, and valid names; absent and present reasons; and Reset. Then check picker interactions separately. Cancel must keep the previous reason both when it is nil and when it has a choice. Choosing the same reason again is still valid and must not create a second picker.

Run the app and record a short sequence: enter Demo Ada, choose Demo chat, open Review, return, reopen the picker, cancel, then Reset. The review and picker should use the same model reference while the root identity is stable. Try an unrelated state change in the root and check that it does not erase the draft. Separately use a deliberate identity-reset wrapper if you want to demonstrate state lifetime; do not conflate that mechanism with the explicit Reset operation.

For the async section, choose success and the fail fixture separately and leave Review during its delay. Explain which task should receive cancellation and why the root's draft remains. The worked lab displays a synthetic result; it does not assert a real request was cancelled at the transport layer. Use controlled service completion in a model test for stale-response evidence.

For visual evidence, inspect longer names, a narrow screen, keyboard visibility, and larger text. A quick fixed-size screenshot is a starting artifact, not a full accessibility review. If snapshot dependencies are absent in the scratch app, do not pretend the repository helper is a standard SwiftUI function you can import anywhere.

sections.title: Find the handoff that caused the symptom
sections.html:
A handoff is where one component passes state or an event to another. If a field changes but the summary stays old, check whether both have the same model and whether body reads the observed property. If typing resets, check identity and model creation inside body. If a picker reopens, check presentation state and callbacks for competing owners. If Cancel changes the reason, look for an unconfirmed highlight written too early.

If the UIKit message remains old, inspect updateUIViewController before blaming Observation. If it has zero height, inspect the represented controller's layout and the parent row's sizing contract. If navigation presents twice, look for work triggered by repeated appearance rather than a guarded flow start. If an old async result appears, inspect freshness checks in both success and failure paths rather than assuming cancel forcibly terminates work.

Use an event notebook with separate columns for model changes, presentation changes, task events, and bridge updates. Print only synthetic information in the scratch app. A screen-level symptom often spans two ownership boundaries; naming those boundaries narrows your search more effectively than adding broad delays or random IDs. A fix should explain the causal chain, not just make the symptom disappear once.

sections.title: Compare the lab with the real demo
sections.html:
A delegate receives events from another object. The address demo owns an observable model in State and also keeps its delegate coordinator alive. The feature view uses Bindable to edit that model. Compare these owners with your root and picker. The production form also normalizes fields, moves focus, reports analytics, and offers a UIKit binding factory. Those are real contracts outside this small lab.

The visit-reason demo enters through a public coordinator instead of constructing the internal feature view. Its invalid empty-input fixture exercises recovery; your small enum-backed picker always has known synthetic choices. The member-ID demo shows both static visual states and a model-driven asynchronous path. Use those examples to understand boundaries, not as a reason to bypass public APIs or put debugging hooks into production flows.

Finish with an engineering note: state the owner of the draft, the modal presentation, the UIKit controller, and the async task; list what survives a push, a return, a Reset, and a process restart. Your draft survives return while the owner identity remains, Reset clears its fields, and a process restart has no persistence contract. This note is the bridge from a working UI to a feature design you can review confidently.

quiz.question: The modal picker should preserve a prior selection when Cancel is tapped. What should its Cancel action do?
options: Always set selectedReason to nil.
Create a new root draft.
Dismiss without changing the committed selection.
quiz.explanation: The lab contract says cancellation preserves current committed state. A temporary tentative selection, if added, should be owned separately and discarded on cancellation.

quiz.question: Why does Review receive the root's model reference instead of copying its fields into State?
options: To share one source of truth and avoid divergent draft copies.
Because every class must be global.
Because State automatically saves models to disk.
quiz.explanation: A shared reference lets all consumers observe the same draft. Local State copies create independent storage and additional synchronization rules; none implies persistence.

quiz.question: The UIKit message does not change after a field edit. Which boundary should you inspect first?
options: The simulator's Wi-Fi configuration.
The representable's update method and its current input.
The enum's CaseIterable implementation.
quiz.explanation: SwiftUI passes updated inputs through the representable update phase. A static or missing update method can leave UIKit rendering old data even when the model is correctly observed.

Selection updates the shared draft; Cancel preserves an existing choice.

exercise.solution:
Try your implementation before using this reference. Put these types in one scratch iOS 17+ module. Include UIKitMessage, DemoLoader, DemoLoadingModel, and DemoLoadingScreen from lessons 010–011. Foundation provides trimming, Observation provides the macro, and SwiftUI provides the controls. The code shows one design; it does not complete your learner task.

import Foundation
import Observation
import SwiftUI

enum PracticeReason: String, CaseIterable, Identifiable {
    case chat = "Demo chat"
    case checkIn = "Demo check-in"
    var id: Self { self }
}

@MainActor
@Observable
final class PracticeDraft {
    var displayName = ""
    var selectedReason: PracticeReason?

    var canReview: Bool {
        !displayName.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty
            && selectedReason != nil
    }

    func reset() {
        displayName = ""
        selectedReason = nil
    }
}

@MainActor
struct PracticeRoot: View {
    @State private var draft = PracticeDraft()
    @State private var showsPicker = false

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            Form {
                Section("Synthetic input") {
                    TextField("Demo display name", text: $draft.displayName)
                    Button(draft.selectedReason?.rawValue ?? "Choose demo reason") {
                        showsPicker = true
                    }
                }
                Section {
                    NavigationLink("Review") {
                        PracticeReview(draft: draft)
                    }
                    .disabled(!draft.canReview)
                    Button("Reset") { draft.reset() }
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Practice draft")
            .sheet(isPresented: $showsPicker) {
                PracticePicker(draft: draft)
            }
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
struct PracticePicker: View {
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss
    let draft: PracticeDraft

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List(PracticeReason.allCases) { reason in
                Button(reason.rawValue) {
                    draft.selectedReason = reason
                    dismiss()
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Demo reason")
            .toolbar {
                Button("Cancel") { dismiss() }
            }
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
struct PracticeReview: View {
    let draft: PracticeDraft
    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Text(draft.selectedReason?.rawValue ?? "No selection")
            UIKitMessage(message: "Demo name: \(draft.displayName)")
                .frame(height: 100)
            DemoLoadingScreen(id: draft.selectedReason?.rawValue ?? "demo-1")
        }
        .navigationTitle("Review")
    }
}

The Boolean conjunction && requires both validity conditions. Root State retains the draft; the picker writes that same object through its plain reference. Bindable is unnecessary here because its buttons assign a property directly rather than requiring a Binding projection. Its Cancel action only dismisses, so an existing choice remains. Review uses ordinary observable reads and a dynamic UIKit message. The modal's separate stack supplies its own toolbar scope. Reset mutates the draft explicitly; it does not use a random ID or replace the stack.

For the failure checkpoint, temporarily pass the literal "fail" to DemoLoadingScreen in your own scratch version, then restore the reason-based input. A model test should assign a whitespace name and a reason and expect false, assign Demo Ada and expect true, call reset and expect empty name, nil reason, and false. The worked code is a reference design inspected for consistency; it is not a claim that an app binary or screenshot was produced.

lessons.title: Feature tracing and review: prove how a screen works
lessons.summary: Follow one user action through the real picker and write a review that separates observed code from unrun checks.
objectives: Follow entry, model, screen, navigation, async work, and result delivery for one feature.
Tell public APIs, project helpers, platform rules, and demo-only hooks apart.
Check strong and weak owners, waits, and cleanup on each ending path.
Write a concrete review and test proposal without treating source inspection as a passed run.

sections.title: Follow one action from start to result
sections.html:
A feature trace explains how a user action produces its result. On Android, you might follow a click, ViewModel intent, repository call, and navigation result. Here choose Open Visit Reason Picker → type a query → select a reason → return a result. Follow Cancel and invalid input too. One connected behavior tells you more than a list of every class in the module.

Start at the demo's ContentView destination, then the wrapper, then the UIKit host, then the public feature coordinator. Mark each boundary: a SwiftUI description becomes a UIKit controller; the host retains a flow owner; the flow owner constructs an internal observable model; a hosted SwiftUI view reads and edits that model; a selection reaches a weak delegate; the owner returns a terminal result. The search action and the selection action take different paths, even though they occur on the same screen.

Record observed implementation separately from inference. Seeing a Task property proves a handle is stored; it does not prove every exit cancels it. Seeing a cancellation test proves that behavior is asserted in source; it does not prove the test passed today. This discipline is especially valuable when entering an unfamiliar platform, because familiar architecture names can create false confidence.

sections.title: Read what the caller is promised
sections.html:
A public contract says what callers outside the module can use. The picker returns an enum: selected with a Procedure, or cancelled. It is public, Equatable, and Sendable. Equatable permits value comparisons. Sendable describes safe transfer under Swift concurrency rules, studied later. Neither saves data or performs navigation or validation. The coordinator also lets callers set analytics context and presentation before starting.

Coordinator<VisitReasonPickerResult, Never> names two type arguments: the result and the thrown failure. The base start method uses throws(Failure), called typed throws. Here Never has no possible values, so start cannot produce a thrown failure through that channel. The caller awaits without try. A cancelled enum result and reported diagnostic errors are still possible. They use other channels.

public permits use outside a module. open additionally permits external subclassing or overriding where applicable. Internal view and model declarations remain hidden from callers. Demo hooks behind #if DEBUG are conditional compilation APIs and are not a general production integration contract. When a proposed change exposes an internal model just to simplify a demo, ask whether the public coordinator or a bounded debug fixture would satisfy that need instead.

sections.title: Map the jobs and the owners
sections.html:
A responsibility map says which component does each job. An ownership map says which component keeps another alive. Keep those meanings separate: using a service does not always mean owning it. For the picker, draw strong arrows for owners and weak arrows for nonowning references. The table shows the current jobs and the source evidence for their lifetimes.

ComponentResponsibilityLifetime evidence
Demo SwiftUI rootExpose entry and display outcomeLocal State stores result and explicit reset identity
UIKit demo hostWait for navigation context and start the flowRetains the feature coordinator
Feature coordinatorConstruct model, choose presentation, return outcomeRetains model, navigation controller, fetch handle, and dismissal adapter
Observable modelQuery text, filtering, optional common-section stateWeak delegate points back to the coordinator
SwiftUI feature viewBind search input and describe rowsUses Bindable on the supplied model
Hosting controllerIntegrate SwiftUI with UIKit navigationRetained by the containing navigation hierarchy

The coordinator's weak hosting-controller reference is not evidence that its screen immediately disappears: the navigation hierarchy retains the hosted controller. Similarly, the model's weak delegate works because the flow has another strong coordinator owner. The modal dismissal adapter must be retained explicitly because assigning a delegate alone is insufficient for its lifetime.

Compare the address feature: a controller can own an observable form model, obtain a hosted controller from bind(), and retain itself or a coordinator as the weak delegate's owner. The Observation macro provides updates; the owner and containment contracts provide lifetime. A review that only checks property wrappers misses half the design.

sections.title: Follow query text into the rows
sections.html:
A derived list is calculated from current inputs instead of kept as another independent list. The picker binds search text to the model. It trims whitespace, combines supported and common procedures while searching, removes duplicate IDs, matches names without case sensitivity, and sorts results. seen.insert($0.id).inserted checks whether an ID was newly added to a Set. That keeps the first occurrence of each ID.

Trace a whitespace-only query separately from an unmatched nonempty query. Whitespace-only input becomes an empty normalized query and preserves the normal list. An unmatched query produces a reversible no-results view. Initializing the whole feature with no supported procedures is different: selection is impossible, so the coordinator reports the invalid invocation and completes cancellation after an alert.

any SomeProtocol holds a conforming value behind a protocol. Parentheses in (any SomeProtocol)? make that whole value optional. try await lookup?.method(...) ?? [] skips a missing lookup and uses an empty array in that case. A thrown failure still leaves this expression for its catch; ?? does not catch it. This feature separately maps optional lookup failure to no suggestions. Check that this fallback fits optional suggestions before using it for required submission data.

sections.title: Read the cleanup on every ending path
sections.html:
A terminal path ends the flow and returns an outcome. Selection reaches the delegate, then the coordinator pops or dismisses and finishes. Explicit result helpers request cancellation of common-suggestion work. Interactive modal dismissal also requests cancellation. The hosting helper recognizes pushed removal when disappearance coincides with isMovingFromParent. Disappearance by itself is not enough evidence that the flow ended.

The pushed-removal callback calls finish(.cancelled). The explicit pop helper first calls fetchTask?.cancel(). Read base finish too: it saves the first result, resumes waiting callers, and clears those waiters. It does not know how to cancel the subclass's stored fetch task. This proves the source paths differ. It does not prove visible harm. Timing, remaining owners, and whether the old model can affect a live screen still need investigation.

A useful review question is whether the feature wants all terminal paths to request cancellation of optional lookup work. Propose a controlled test that starts the lookup, simulates actual pushed removal, then completes the lookup and observes cancellation or the intended no-update policy. This is more precise than a broad instruction to add weak self everywhere.

Finally, result storage defensively accepts only the first finish. The base's documented caller contract still says to finish once. First-result protection prevents duplicate delivery; it does not make repeated result-producing paths a good design. Explicit selection disables its removal callback before popping so the two outcomes do not compete.

sections.title: Ask what each existing test actually exercises
sections.html:
Test coverage is the behavior the checks exercise, not just the files they mention. Model tests cover whitespace, case-insensitive filtering, no match, and selection events. Coordinator tests cover push, selected and cancelled results, optional lookup, modal callbacks, and invalid input. Snapshots show default, filtered, and no-results states. The UI test checks the invalid-input alert and cancellation. Read the test stimulus before judging the strength of that evidence.

Read how each test stimulates the behavior. The modal interaction test invokes the presentation delegate callback directly. That verifies callback integration and returned result, but does not itself perform a real swipe gesture through UIKit animation. The invalid-input unit test uses a special presenter because a scene-less test host may not deliver transition completion like a running app. The UI test supplies separate end-to-end evidence for that alert path.

For a proposed change, name the failing requirement and the test boundary that would detect it. Query normalization should need a model assertion, not a new app-launch test. Shared error styling might need a snapshot. Gesture and container integration may need both a helper test and a focused UI path. Report planned checks as planned until executed, and preserve accepted baselines until an understood rendering change merits review.

sections.title: Write a review with a trigger and a check
sections.html:
A review finding links a concrete trigger to a consequence and a proposed check. For example, the pushed-removal callback finishes while an optional lookup may still be waiting. It does not use the explicit cancellation helper. Ask whether lookup should stop on that path, and propose a controlled pending-lookup test. The code shows a difference in cleanup. It does not alone prove harm to the user.

For ownership findings, name the cycle or missing retained owner. For state findings, name both conflicting sources. For concurrency findings, name the suspension point and the assumption that may become stale. For API findings, identify which caller's contract changes. Avoid turning familiar Android advice into a universal iOS rule: a received ObservableObject, an owner-created Observable model, and a UIKit flow coordinator all have different integration requirements.

Keep platform availability accurate. SwiftUI Observation integration begins with iOS 17-era APIs; this demo's target minimum is iOS 18.2. That does not imply every module or production app has the same minimum. The member-ID model still follows ObservableObject conventions in this checkout, while the address and picker models use Observation. A review should honor those actual declarations and describe a migration explicitly if one is proposed.

sections.title: Recall the connected rules without the text
sections.html:
Recall means explaining the idea without looking at the lesson. Why can an appearing controller be the same object? Why can a new SwiftUI description keep State? Why does Bindable not establish an owner? Why does await not mean background execution? Then explain how a flow can return cancelled while its thrown-failure type is Never. Connect each answer to a specific mechanism.

Next, predict what happens if the picker demo generates a new ID on every body evaluation, if its host does not retain the coordinator, if the weak model delegate has no other owner, or if a cancelled lookup still publishes a result. For each prediction, name the boundary and the smallest useful observation or test. Do not repair every issue with another wrapper or another Task; choose a change that restores the violated contract.

Your final artifact should be a one-page feature trace with an outcome table, an ownership map, current test coverage, one evidence-backed review question, and verification limits. You are ready for the data and concurrency unit when you can defend that trace using source and API semantics without assuming that familiar architecture vocabulary guarantees identical platform behavior.

quiz.question: A coordinator specializes Failure as Never. Which statement is correct?
options: Its flow cannot return cancelled or show an error alert.
Its declared thrown-error channel cannot produce a Failure, but cancelled can still be a normal result.
The process can never terminate.
quiz.explanation: Never concerns the specialized failure channel. The selected/cancelled result enum and diagnostic reporting are separate from thrown errors.

quiz.question: The pushed-removal callback calls finish(.cancelled). Why inspect the base finish implementation?
options: To determine whether finish also cancels subclass-owned tasks before claiming uniform cleanup.
Because finish always deallocates its caller immediately.
Because weak references trigger finish automatically.
quiz.explanation: The base stores and delivers a result; it does not automatically know about the subclass's fetch handle. Cleanup claims require tracing the actual implementation.

quiz.question: A test directly invokes presentationControllerDidDismiss. What does it establish?
options: A real swipe gesture and every animation path passed.
Every navigation controller is safe to dismiss.
The delegate callback path returns the expected result under that test fixture.
quiz.explanation: Direct callback stimulation gives focused integration evidence. It does not replace a real-gesture or container-animation check when that behavior is material.

exercise.solution:
The worked trace follows one result. The demo creates a wrapper; the wrapper creates a UIKit host. The host waits for navigation containment, retains the coordinator, and awaits start. The coordinator validates input and owns the model. The hosted view edits that model. Selection reaches its delegate; the coordinator moves the controller and returns selected. The demo shows the result. No matches keeps the picker active. Invalid starting input returns cancelled after an alert.

The outcome table must show explicit pop/dismiss helpers requesting fetch cancellation, interactive modal dismissal requesting cancellation, and the pushed-removal callback delivering cancellation directly. The base finish stores the first result and resumes waiters; cancellation of subclass tasks is not part of that implementation. The defensively protected first result does not weaken the documented finish-once contract.

A review question can read: should pushed gesture removal also request cancellation of common-suggestion lookup work? The source shows different cleanup paths; add a fake lookup that signals start, trigger removal, then complete the lookup to verify the intended policy. Report this as a policy and verification question unless you have demonstrated harmful behavior. Contrast the direct-delegate modal test with an actual gesture run.

The address comparison should name State ownership, Bindable field access, weak delegate retention, batch prefill suppression, and caller-owned hosted containment. The platform note should name iOS 17 Observation integration, this demo's iOS 18.2 target, and the legacy ObservableObject member-ID model. No client modifications or test execution are implied by completing this reading exercise.

simple.story: A parcel depot has a public counter, a sorting desk, a van, and a receipt desk. Ravi follows one parcel rather than listing every room. He watches the counter accept it, the sorter choose a route, and the receipt desk record delivery or cancellation. He also checks who holds the parcel while the van waits. One exit closes the receipt and tells the driver to stop. Another closes the receipt without telling the driver. Ravi can describe that difference from the written instructions.
